User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — that’s a good set of facts. I can give a clear plan and initial guidance, but I need two quick clarifying questions before I finalize calculations and a firm recommendation:

1) Is the $5,100 of student-loan interest paid in 2024 (i.e., interest you actually paid during tax year 2024)? Or is that the total interest paid in 2018–2021 (which would not be deductible on your 2024 return)?  
2) Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expense

s for your photography work (supplies, travel, advertising, etc.) or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from a job?

Answering those will change how much you can deduct and whether some items belong on Schedule C vs. being nondeductible.

Below is a clear summary of how each item is treated, whether you should likely itemize, and which forms you’ll need.

Summary of how to treat each income and deduction
- W-2 (Coastal Manufacturing) $68,200: Report on Form 1040 (W-2 income). Withholding on your W-2 af

fects whether you’ll owe estimated tax; include it on Form 1040.
- Self-employment (photography) $16,300: Report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). Income minus ordinary and necessary business expenses = net profit (or loss). Net profit is subject to income tax and self-employment (SE) tax.
  - Business expenses (if the $1,050 are business-related) are deductible on Schedule C against the $16,300.
  - Home office deduction (see below) is also a Schedule C deduction (either directly via the simpli

fied method or via Form 8829 if using the regular method).
- Interest/dividends: Capital One 360 $2,100 and Merrill Edge $420 — generally reportable as interest/dividend income on Form 1040.
  - Because total interest and dividends exceed $1,500, you will likely need Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).
- Student loan interest $5,100 (Nelnet): Student-loan interest deduction is an above-the-line adjustment (reduces AGI) up to a maximum of $2,500 for the tax year — but it phases out for higher MAGI.

Important: it’s only for interest you actually paid in the tax year. If the $5,100 was paid in earlier years, it is not deductible on your 2024 return.
- Charitable contributions $1,500 (Salvation Army with receipt): Charitable gifts are an itemized deduction (Schedule A). They are not available if you take the standard deduction (except for any special-year adjustments that may have applied previously — typically not in normal years).
- Unreimbursed employee expenses $1,050: Post‑TCJA (2018–2025), unreimb

ursed employee business expenses are not deductible for most employees. If these are business expenses for your self-employment (photography), they go on Schedule C and are deductible. If they are employee unreimbursed expenses, they are NOT deductible on your federal return.

Home office deduction
- You said: exclusive home office area = 120 sq ft; total home 740 sq ft; rent $1,750/month (annual rent = $1,750 × 12 = $21,000).
- Two methods:
  1) Simplified method: $5.00 per square foot up to 300 sq ft → 12

0 × $5 = $600 deduction.
  2) Regular method: business-use percentage = 120 / 740 ≈ 16.22%. Deduct that percentage of allowable home expenses (rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, homeowner’s insurance portion, repairs allocable to the office). With just rent alone: 0.1622 × $21,000 ≈ $3,405. If you have utilities and insurance, the deductible amount increases above $3,405.
- Recommendation: Regular method will likely give you a larger deduction here (≈$3,405 from rent alone vs. $600 simplified), so use the

regular method if you plan to keep good records of rent/utilities and if your home office is used regularly and exclusively for the business. You’ll claim the regular-method allocation on Form 8829 (if net profit; the deduction is taken on Schedule C). Note: home-office deductions cannot create or increase a business loss that offsets W-2 wages — they can only offset business income (there are loss carryover rules for passive loss limits).

Self-employment tax and related adjustments
- Net self-employment

income (Schedule C profit) is subject to self-employment tax (~15.3% on ~92.35% of net earnings). You compute SE tax on Schedule SE. You can deduct one-half of the SE tax as an adjustment on Form 1040 (above the line).
- You may also be eligible for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) 20% deduction (Section 199A) for pass-through income from your photography business — this depends on taxable income and the nature of the business, but many single filers with modest business income qualify for some or all of

the 20% deduction. The QBI deduction is claimed on Form 1040 (using Form 8995 or 8995-A as needed).

Standard deduction vs. itemize
- Standard deduction (single): If you don’t have significant other itemizable deductions (mortgage interest, large property taxes, large medical expenses above threshold, etc.), you will likely be better off taking the standard deduction. With only $1,500 in charitable giving and Texas having no state income tax (so no state income tax deduction), it’s unlikely your itemized d

eductions exceed the standard deduction unless you have mortgage interest, property taxes, or other itemizable expenses you haven’t listed.
- Student loan interest is an above-the-line deduction and does NOT affect the itemize vs standard decision.
- Quick decision rule: add up likely itemizable items (charity $1,500 + property taxes + mortgage interest + other allowable deductions). If that total exceeds the single standard deduction for 2024 (check the IRS publication for the exact inflation-adjusted numb

er or I can look it up for you), itemize; otherwise take the standard deduction.

Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return) — main form.
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — if you have adjustments such as deductible part of self-employment tax or student-loan interest (depending on software you might not see Schedule 1 directly, but the data flows into 1040).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report photography income and expenses.
- Schedule SE

— to compute self-employment tax.
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (if you use the regular method for the home office).
- Schedule B — if interest/dividend income > $1,500 or if you have certain foreign accounts.
- Form 8995 or 8995-A — if you claim the QBI (20%) deduction (Form depends on complexity/income level).
- Form 1098-E — student loan interest statement (you’ll need the amount the lender reports for the year if you paid interest in 2024).
- 1099-NEC or 1099-NEC / 1099-NEC-equiv

alent or 1099-K — for self-employment payments, if any were issued to you.
- Keep receipts/invoices for business expenses, charitable receipts, records of rent/utilities for the home office, and all 1099s/W-2s.

Practical example (illustrative) — shows why regular home-office method may help
- Gross self-employment income: $16,300
- Suppose business expenses (supplies, mileage, etc.): $1,050 (if those are business expenses)
- Regular home-office allocation (rent only): ≈ $3,405
- Net Schedule C profit estim

ate = 16,300 − 1,050 − 3,405 = 11,845
- SE tax (rough) ≈ 15.3% × (0.9235 × 11,845) ≈ $1,674; half of that ≈ $837 is an above-the-line deduction.
- This example is only illustrative — actual numbers depend on exact deductible expenses and whether the $1,050 is business-related and whether you have additional allowable home costs (utilities, insurance, repairs) to include.

Other important notes
- Student loan interest phase-out: the student-loan interest deduction phases out above certain MAGI limits — the d

eduction can be reduced or eliminated depending on your modified AGI. Because your combined income from W-2 + interest + self-employment might push MAGI into the phase-out range, your deductible portion could be reduced. I can estimate phase-out once you confirm the actual interest paid in 2024 and other specifics.
- Estimated taxes: because of self-employment income you may need to make quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) if your W-2 withholding doesn’t cover your total tax liability. You generally

should make estimated payments if you expect to owe $1,000+ after withholding.
- State taxes: You live in Texas — Texas has no state income tax, so nothing to file at the state level for wages. (Local property tax may affect itemizing, but that’s a federal itemized deduction limited by SALT cap of $10,000.)

What I recommend you do next
1. Answer my two clarifying questions above (student-loan interest timing and whether the $1,050 are business expenses).  
2. Gather documents: W-2, any 1099-NEC / 1099-K /

1099-MISC, 1099-INT / 1099-DIV, 1098-E (student loan interest received for 2024), receipts for charitable gifts, receipts and records for photography business expenses (including mileage logs if relevant), rent and utility bills for the home so we can allocate accurately.  
3. If you want, I can compute a near-final tax estimate (taxable income, self-employment tax, whether QBI applies, and whether you should itemize) once you confirm the clarifications and provide any additional itemizable items (mortgage

interest, property tax, large medical expenses, etc.).

If you want, say “Yes — compute estimate” and provide answers to the two questions (and any other deductions like mortgage interest or property tax), and I’ll produce a line-by-line estimate and a recommendation whether to itemize or take the standard deduction.
